sentence: The NHS uses the FAST test to describe the main signs of a stroke.
note: FAST named in summary of NHS pages

sentence: FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999.
note: FAST (face, arms, speech, time to call 999)

sentence: Face weakness can make one side of the face droop, and arm weakness can stop a person keeping both arms raised.
note: Face weakness/droop; arm weakness cannot keep both arms raised

sentence: Other signs include weakness or numbness down one side of the body, blurred vision, and confusion and memory loss.
note: Other signs listed in the summary

sentence: Symptoms can pass quickly, but the NHS says medical help should be sought straight away even if they stop.
note: Symptoms can pass quickly; even if they stop, seek help straight away

sentence: A stroke needs urgent medical help in hospital because it can be life-threatening, so the route is to call 999.
note: A stroke needs urgent medical help in hospital; can be life-threatening

sentence: A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, causes symptoms like those of a stroke that pass within minutes or hours.
note: TIA symptoms mirror a stroke's but pass within minutes or hours

sentence: During a TIA it is not possible to tell whether it is a TIA or a full stroke, so the advice is to call 999 even if things improve.
Most strokes are ischaemic, which means the blood supply is stopped by a blood clot.
note: Most strokes ischaemic, blood supply stopped by clot

sentence: Haemorrhagic strokes happen when a weakened blood vessel supplying the brain bursts.
note: Haemorrhagic strokes occur when weakened vessel bursts

sentence: Bleeding can be within brain tissue, which is called intracerebral, or around the surface of the brain, which is called subarachnoid.
note: intracerebral (within brain tissue) or subarachnoid (around surface)

sentence: A TIA is sometimes called a mini-stroke because the symptoms are temporary.
note: temporary version of stroke symptoms, often called mini-stroke

sentence: The WHO says a TIA usually lasts only a few minutes and causes no long-term damage.
note: WHO: usually a few minutes, no long-term damage

sentence: The CDC describes a TIA as a warning sign of a future stroke, so it needs urgent assessment.
note: CDC: TIA warning sign of future stroke; urgent assessment

sentence: Some sources treat a TIA as separate from the main stroke types rather than as a type of stroke.
note: CDC lists only two types; UK sources list all three

sentence: Risk rises with diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and irregular heartbeats such as atrial fibrillation.
Diagnosis in hospital involves blood tests, brain scans and other tests to confirm a stroke and find its cause.
note: blood tests, CT scans and other tests

sentence: Brain scans show whether a blocked artery or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected, and how severe it is.
note: scans show clot or bleed, area, severity

sentence: NHS inform says the two main types of brain scan are computerised tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
note: 2 main types of brain scan CT and MRI

sentence: The type of scan depends on the symptoms.
Some people have both, and may need further scans that are good at showing the blood vessels in the brain.
The Stroke Association advises that a brain scan is done soon after symptoms start.
An electrocardiogram (ECG) checks the heart, and ultrasound scans can look in and around the brain.
note: ECG to check heart; ultrasound in and around brain

sentence: Hospitals also commonly check for diabetes and high cholesterol, and may use an ultrasound of the neck arteries called a carotid Doppler.
Treatment depends on the type of stroke.
note: This depends on the stroke type

sentence: In the first 24 hours it may include clot-dissolving medicine, surgery to remove a clot, or procedures to relieve pressure in the skull.
note: thrombolysis, thrombectomy, procedures to relieve pressure

sentence: The Stroke Association says thrombolysis uses a clot-busting medicine to break up clots and restore blood flow.
note: thrombolysis breaks up clots, restores blood flow

sentence: Thrombectomy removes the blood clot to help reduce brain damage by restoring blood flow.
It is used for people whose stroke is caused by a blockage in the large arteries of the brain.
Rapid treatment is important because the benefit of thrombectomy falls over time.
Clot-dissolving medicine cannot be given to everyone, for example where there are significant bleeding risks.
note: summary said alteplase cannot be given with significant bleeding risks; attribution to this page uncertain

sentence: Longer-term medicines often include anticoagulants to stop blood clots forming, medicines to lower blood pressure, and statins to lower cholesterol.
The Stroke Association says most people who have an ischaemic stroke are given blood-thinning medication to help prevent clots.
The NHS says recovery time varies widely.
For some people it may take days or weeks and have little impact on life.
For others it can take months or years and may mean making life changes.
Rehabilitation from physiotherapists, speech and occupational therapists and others is central to progress.
Physiotherapy aims to restore functional movement and reduce impairment.
Speech and language therapists assess and treat swallowing, speech, language and communication problems.
They also assess swallowing and recommend ways to make eating and drinking as safe as possible.
Rehabilitation often starts in hospital or a local clinic and may continue at home.
Community stroke teams can work with people where they live.
Typical teams also include dietitians, psychologists, and specialist nurses and doctors.
Swallowing difficulties can lead to a lung infection called pneumonia when liquid is breathed into the lungs.
Poor circulation and reduced mobility can lead to deep vein thrombosis, which is a clot in a leg vein.
note: DVT from poor circulation and reduced mobility

sentence: The WHO also lists pressure ulcers, limb contracture, spasticity and shoulder pain as possible complications.
Problems with language can affect speaking, understanding, reading and writing, and this is called aphasia or dysphasia.
NHS inform lists depression and anxiety as common after a stroke, along with anger, frustration and sudden laughing or crying.
It says tiredness can be severe and long-lasting, and can last months or even years.
The Stroke Association says at least one third of stroke survivors have some form of depression within the first year.
note: leaflet: at least one third; first year

sentence: It advises that low mood can be raised with a stroke nurse or GP, and gives its helpline as 0303 3033 100.
note: speak to stroke nurse or GP; helpline number

sentence: FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999, the NHS says.
Face weakness can make one side of the face droop, and arm weakness can stop a person keeping both arms raised.
Symptoms can pass quickly, but the NHS says medical help should be sought straight away even if they stop.
A TIA has symptoms like those of a stroke, but they pass within minutes or hours.

The CDC describes a TIA as a warning sign of a future stroke.

The type of scan depends on the symptoms, and some people have both.
The scans show whether a blocked artery or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke and which part of the brain is affected.

For some people it takes days or weeks, with little impact on life.
For others it can take months or years and may mean making life changes.
Rehabilitation from physiotherapists, speech and occupational therapists and others is central to progress.
NHS inform lists depression and anxiety as common after a stroke, along with anger, frustration and sudden laughing or crying.
The Stroke Association says depression can also appear later or return.
note: leaflet: can appear later, return over and over
